business.title: COS for business
business.intro: COS is a Company Operating System. It connects people, processes, data, software, automation and AI so the company can operate as one controlled system rather than a collection of unrelated tools.
business.summary: At a practical level, COS should answer five questions: what is happening now, who owns it, what should happen next, what facts are required, and where a human decision is needed.
business.problemText: Companies usually accumulate separate tools faster than they accumulate a shared operating model. Sales live in a CRM, documents in storage, tasks elsewhere, agreements in messengers, while critical business logic often exists only in people's heads.
business.problem2: employees copy the same facts between several systems;
business.problem3: processes depend on specific people and fail when context is lost;
business.problem4: automation performs isolated actions without understanding the whole process;
business.problem5: AI lacks structured context or clear authority boundaries;
business.problem6: after a failure it is difficult to reconstruct who did what and why.
business.gain1: one operational picture across processes, clients, assets, tasks, decisions and events;
business.gain2: explicit process stages, ownership, transition rules and exceptions;
business.gain3: automation with policies, limits and human approvals where required;
business.gain4: AI that works with company state, facts, rules, history and bounded authority;
business.gain5: traceable decisions, execution history and measurable outcomes.
business.notText: COS is not trying to become another CRM, accounting package, file storage product or messenger. It can use and connect those systems. Its role is to know the operating process, state, rules and responsibility, and coordinate execution across people, software and AI.
business.fitText: COS is most useful where several teams or business areas already interact, repeatable processes matter, multiple information systems exist, and manual coordination has become a visible operating cost.
business.nextText: Continue with the capabilities, practical use cases or the implementation route.

integrators.title: COS for implementation professionals
integrators.intro: This section is for business analysts, integrators, implementation leads and technical specialists who turn COS from a software product into an operating model for a real company.
integrators.principle: Do not start with screens and settings. First understand the process, data, responsibility and decision points. Automated chaos is still chaos, it just moves faster.
integrators.sequence4: map business objects and critical facts;
integrators.sequence5: identify systems of record and external services;
integrators.sequence6: define rules, approvals, exceptions and failures;
integrators.sequence7: decide what remains human, what is automated and what can use AI;
integrators.resultText: The result is not a collection of configured forms. It is an explicit operating model with process purpose, ownership, critical facts, systems of record, automation boundaries, human approvals, failure handling and measurable success criteria.
integrators.technicalTitle: When to move to technical documentation
integrators.technicalText: Once the process and integration model are clear, continue to the developer section for architecture boundaries, code, APIs, events, tests and executable contracts.

developers.title: COS for developers
developers.intro: This is the technical entry point to COS. Domain-owned business meaning is separated from generic execution mechanisms. Domains own vocabulary, state and business rules; the Kernel provides reusable execution, event, policy, extension and observability mechanisms.
developers.principleText: Business meaning belongs to a domain. Generic execution, events, policies, extensions and observability belong to shared runtime mechanisms. A change should preserve that boundary instead of hiding domain behavior inside infrastructure.
developers.before1: identify who semantically owns the new behavior;
developers.before2: decide whether it is a domain capability or a generic mechanism;
developers.before3: identify the business process being changed;
developers.before4: identify affected commands, events and contracts;
developers.before5: check whether the external API changes;
developers.before6: define tests that prove the behavior;
developers.before7: synchronize the documentation and generated reference.
